title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
hook: Krishna is about to leave the world, and his friend asks for one thing: take me with you

segments.voice: Last week took each as a lens for a week: six schools, six ways of seeing, none of them ranked. Which lens stayed with you? Now the lineage track comes back, starting on the path of action. Day one thousand two hundred two.
screen: `SIX LENSES, NONE RANKED.` · `NOW, THE PATH OF ACTION.`

segments.voice: Krishna is about to leave the world. In the Bhagavata's eleventh book, the gods come to remind him that his work on earth is done, and his own clan is heading toward its end. Uddhava hears it: his close friend, the learned messenger who once carried his words to Vraja. He comes to Krishna alone and asks for one thing: take me with you. He says he can't bear to be apart from him. What Krishna gives him instead is a long teaching. Tradition calls it the Uddhava Gita. This week, the path of karma, action, reads it from the start.
screen: `KRISHNA IS ABOUT TO LEAVE.` → `TAKE ME WITH YOU.` → `WHAT HE GETS INSTEAD: A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Krishna's first answer sounds hard. Don't follow me, he says. When I'm gone, let go of your attachment to family and friends, fix your mind on me, and wander the earth seeing everything evenly. Uddhava doesn't pretend. He says, in effect: this kind of letting go is hard for people like me, whose minds cling to the body and to what is ours. Teach me how. And Krishna does. That's the shape of the whole Uddhava Gita: an honest question, then a teacher who stays to answer it, chapter after chapter, before he goes. Why read it on the path of action? Because Uddhava isn't a sage in a cave. He's a man with duties, a household, a city, and a friend about to be gone. His question is the karma question: how do I keep acting in a world that keeps losing things? The answers in the next few days come at action from several sides: what to learn from the people who wrong you, which path suits whom, where joy and sorrow really come from, and how to work without hurry. One more thing to notice before we start. Krishna doesn't take Uddhava with him. The teacher leaves, and the student keeps living. The teaching is what's left to carry. Karma, in this book, starts right there: with the work a person does after the one they leaned on is gone.
screen: `DON'T FOLLOW ME. LET GO, AND WANDER.` · `THIS IS HARD FOR ME. TEACH ME HOW.` · `THE KARMA QUESTION: HOW DO I KEEP ACTING?` · `THE TEACHER LEAVES; THE STUDENT LIVES ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with what you were handed. Settle, and let the breath slow down on its own. Bring to mind someone who taught you something and isn't here to ask anymore: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who moved away. Don't reach for the loss. Reach for one thing they left you: a habit, a saying, a way of doing an ordinary job. Hold that one thing for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can offer that person and that gift to the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, work, the deed itself. In the Uddhava Gita it begins with one honest question: how to keep acting when the one you leaned on is leaving. Today's word.
Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Today, do one small task the way someone who taught you would have done it, and let it be yours now. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: Students of the Bhagavata Purana read the eleventh book's long dialogue between Krishna and Uddhava, known as the Uddhava Gita, as a teaching in its own right, and it is recited along with the rest of the Purana when the whole text is read aloud.

fork.setup: you're Uddhava. your friend Krishna is about to leave the world. what do you ask him for?
options: a kingdom to look after once he's gone.
to be taken along with him.
fork.reveal: Uddhava asks to go with him. Krishna says no, and then stays to teach him. that teaching is the Uddhava Gita.

original.note: Sanskrit: action, work, deed. the path of karma is the path of action.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is what comes back around to you.
what it means: action itself, and here, Uddhava's question of how to keep acting when the teacher is leaving.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 11.6–7: the gods' visit, Uddhava's plea, and Krishna's first answer, opening the dialogue tradition calls the Uddhava Gita.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.6 (the gods ask Krishna to return; Uddhava comes to him privately and asks to be taken along)
Bhagavata Purana 11.7.1–18 (Krishna tells Uddhava to give up attachment and wander with his mind on him; Uddhava says this is hard and asks to be taught)
Bhagavata Purana 10.46–47 (Uddhava as messenger to Vraja, recalled)

notes: Opens the year-four lineage track (karma strand) and a new week (week 21 of year four, days 1202–1208). The review was written from the index for days 1197–1201 ('each as a lens for a week'), whose scripts were not on disk when this was written; editor checked it against them and it holds.

Editor pass: smoothed a fragment in the hook ('Uddhava hears. Uddhava, his close friend...') and cut 'spread across many chapters' (an unsourced count-like claim); the teach already says 'chapter after chapter'.
'Uddhava Gita' is the traditional name for Krishna's teaching to Uddhava in Bhagavata book 11; confirm the usual chapter range (commonly given as 11.6 or 11.7 through 11.29).

Paraphrase of 11.6–7: the gods' request, the coming end of the Yadu clan, Uddhava's plea, Krishna's instruction to renounce and wander, and Uddhava's reply that this is hard for those attached to body and kin. Confirm verse ranges and wording.
Uddhava described only as Krishna's close friend; he is often called a cousin and counselor as well. Left out as unneeded.
howItsDone refers to recitation of the whole Purana (e.g. Bhagavata saptaha) without naming a count; confirm wording.
'Karma' glossed as action, work, deed (a translation, not an etymology).
